senses.gloss: Kaulakāvatī are two persons mentioned in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (ii. 1, 3) as having given advice, in the capacity of priests, to rathaprota dārbhya.

Kaulāla is a word denoting a hereditary potter (‘son of a kulāla or potter’) according to the commentator Mahīdhara on the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā. The other Samhitās have kulāla.
Foot notes xxx. 7.
Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 9, 5; kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvii. 13, and cf. Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 27.

Kaulitara is mentioned in the Rigveda as a dāsa. Apparently the name is an epithet of śambara, meaning ‘son of Kulitara’: this points to śambara having been a terrestrial foe, and not a mere demon.
Foot notes iv. 30. 14.
Cf. Hillebrandt, Vedische Mythologie, 3, 273; Macdonell, Vedic Mythology, pp. 64, 161.

Kaulīka, like kulīkā, is the name of some sort of bird in the list of victims at the aśvamedha, or horse sacrifice, in the yajurveda.
Foot notes Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 24; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 5.
